purpose: Heparin is a blood thinner used to prevent or treat dangerous blood clots in your veins, arteries, or lungs. It is also used during certain medical procedures like surgeries or dialysis to keep your blood from clotting in tubes and equipment. Doctors may also use it to treat a heart attack or serious clotting conditions.
how_it_works: Your blood naturally has proteins that help it clot to stop bleeding. Heparin works by blocking some of those clotting proteins so your blood takes longer to form a clot. Think of it as putting a slowdown signal on your blood's clotting system so dangerous clots cannot form or grow bigger.
common_side_effects: The most common side effect is bleeding, which can show up as unusual bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, or blood in your urine or stool. You may also notice some pain, redness, or irritation at the injection site. Some people experience a drop in their platelet count, which your doctor will monitor with blood tests.
warnings: Because heparin thins your blood, even a small cut can bleed more than usual, so be careful with sharp objects and contact sports. Tell your doctor right away if you notice unexpected or heavy bleeding anywhere on your body. A rare but serious reaction called HIT (Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia) can actually cause dangerous clots, so your platelet levels will be checked regularly while you are on this medicine.
typical_dosing: Heparin is always given by injection — either into a vein (IV) through a drip or as a shot under the skin. It is never taken by mouth as a pill. Your dose is carefully calculated based on your weight and the reason you need it, and it is closely monitored with regular blood tests called PTT or anti-Xa levels to make sure it is working safely.
